newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israel, PLO meet in Cairo to revive Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO meet in Cairo to revive Mideast peace.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met on Sunday for the first time in more than two months to lay the groundwork for restarting peace talks stalled over Jewish settlement building on occupied Arab lands.

The negotiators did not speak to reporters before they started meeting at the Ittihadia presidential palace in Cairo. Egyptian presidential adviser Osama el-Baz, who has been mediating between the two sides to revive peacemaking, also attended the talks.
Palestinian-Israeli peace talks abruptly halted in March when Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement at the Jerusalem hillside known as Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa.

Israeli Ambassador to Egypt Zvi Mazael told reporters earlier that his country's delegation was hopeful but senior Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said he was not expecting much from the Cairo meeting.
"We should not raise our expectations about the meeting. The gap between the two sides is greater than many people may expect," Erekat told reporters.

"We hope Mr Netanyahu and his government will take a decision to freeze all settlement activity so we can put the peace process back on track. He knows what the obstacles to peace are, all he has to do is look in the mirror."

The Palestinians insist Israel must stop its settlement activity before they can restart serious peace talks but Netanyahu's 66-54 majority in parliament could crumble if he stopped the Jewish housing projects, which are backed by religious and right-wing legislators in his government.

Israeli officials have consistently ruled out any halt to settlement building but on Sunday Israel's Channel One television said Netanyahu might be considering a clandestine end to the Jerusalem settlement.

It quoted European Union envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos as saying that Netanyahu told Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, he would check into a possible halt to the housing project without making any official announcement but that he would also take into consideration his coalition.

But Netanyahu appeared to have little hope of convincing his government. On Sunday his education minister, whose National Religious Party (NRP) holds nine seats in parliament, was quoted as saying the settlement building would not stop.

Settler leader Pinchas Wallerstein also told Israel's Channel Two television: "He (Netanyahu) cannot, with this government, freeze settlement...I do not think he wants to freeze it. But if he is pressed to do it, he will have to change his government."

Egypt, which considers itself an unofficial sponsor of the peace talks, has intensified its role in the peace crisis since a summit between Mubarak and Netanyahu last month. Analysts say it has even replaced the United States as the main mediator.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat held talks with Mubarak on Saturday as part of their ongoing consultations. On Sunday, the Palestinian leader met Jordan's King Hussein in Amman to review the latest Egyptian moves to revive peace.

Diplomatic sources say Egypt is pushing a five-point plan which included a freeze on any change in the status of Jerusalem and a ban on Jewish settlement building in the West Bank for "a sufficient period". In return the Palestinians would give a firm commitment to address Israel's security demands.
